tagline: A grand duchy of castles and bankers
overview:
Luxembourg is a small landlocked country in Western Europe, tucked between Belgium, Germany, and France. It is about the size of Rhode Island, small enough to drive across in under an hour, yet it is one of the richest countries in the world per person. The capital, Luxembourg City, is perched dramatically on cliffs above two river gorges, with old fortress walls, bridges, and casemates, tunnels carved into the rock, giving it the nickname Gibraltar of the North.

About 670,000 people live in Luxembourg, and nearly half of them are foreign citizens, the highest share in the European Union; another 200,000 people commute in every day from neighboring countries to work. Luxembourgers speak three languages: Luxembourgish, a Germanic language, at home, plus French and German in school, government, and business. The country is a grand duchy, the world's only one, meaning its head of state is a grand duke, with an elected parliament running the government. Luxembourg is a founding member of the European Union and hosts several of its institutions, and its economy runs on banking, investment funds, steel, and satellites.
landAndNature: Luxembourg has two distinct halves. The north, called the Oesling, is part of the Ardennes plateau, a rugged region of forested hills, deep river valleys, and castle-topped villages, rising to about 560 meters at Kneiff, the highest point. The south, the Gutland or good land, is gentler and more fertile, with farms, orchards, and towns. Along the eastern border the Moselle River flows past steep vineyards that produce crisp white wines. The Mullerthal region, nicknamed Little Switzerland, is a maze of sandstone rock formations, narrow crevices, and mossy forest trails. Forests cover about a third of the country and hold red deer, wild boar, and wildcats, and the Our and Sûre rivers wind through quiet valleys. The climate is mild and fairly wet.
peopleAndCulture: Luxembourgers switch easily among Luxembourgish, French, German, and often English or Portuguese, since a large Portuguese community has lived here for decades. Most people are Roman Catholic. National dishes include judd mat gaardebounen, smoked pork collar with broad beans, and gromperekichelcher, crispy potato fritters sold at fairs; the country is also proud of its Moselle wines and sparkling crémant. On the eve of National Day, June 23, the capital fills with fireworks and street parties. The Schueberfouer, a funfair founded in 1340, still takes over the city each summer, and the Echternach hopping procession, where thousands skip through the streets, is a UNESCO tradition. Cycling and soccer are popular, and Luxembourg has produced Tour de France winners.
history: Luxembourg began in 963 when Count Siegfried acquired a small castle on a rock called Lucilinburhuc, the little fortress. His descendants became dukes, and in the 1300s the House of Luxembourg produced four Holy Roman Emperors. The fortress city was so strong that Burgundians, Spanish, French, Austrians, and Prussians fought to hold it for 400 years. In 1815 Luxembourg became a grand duchy under the Dutch king, and it gained full independence in 1867 on condition that it tear down its fortress and stay neutral. Germany occupied it in both world wars, and the Battle of the Bulge raged across its north in 1944 and 1945. After the war Luxembourg helped found NATO, the European Union, and the Benelux customs union, and it became a center of European banking and institutions.
funFacts: Luxembourg was the first country in the world to make all public transportation free, in 2020.
Nearly half of Luxembourg's residents are foreign citizens, and more than 170 nationalities live in the country.
Luxembourg is the only grand duchy left in the world, ruled by a grand duke rather than a king or prince.
The capital's Bock casemates are 17 kilometers of tunnels carved into the cliffs, once holding soldiers, horses, and bakeries.
Luxembourg has the most Michelin-starred restaurants per person of any country in the world.
